claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are equiatomic PtPdRhIrAu nanoparticles with a homogeneous solid-solution structure.
The initial solid solution is disordered and has no elemental segregation.
Differences in the constituent metals' surface energies drive temperature-induced surface segregation.
Temperature-induced surface segregation undermines the solid-solution structure at catalytic and thermoelectric operating temperatures.
Elevated temperature enhances atomic mobility in the nanoparticles.
Metals with lower surface energy preferentially migrate toward the nanoparticle surface.
Preferential migration produces compositional gradients and phase separation in uncoated nanoparticles.
An ultrathin inert shell physically restricts surface diffusion.
Restricting surface diffusion with an inert shell preserves the original high-entropy solid solution at elevated temperatures.
Uncoated PtPdRhIrAu nanoparticles will segregate after annealing between 473 K and 1923 K.
Segregation in uncoated nanoparticles will be especially pronounced under oxidizing conditions.
Alumina-coated PtPdRhIrAu nanoparticles will retain a uniform solid-solution structure after the same annealing treatments.
Entropy-induced high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics can maintain uniform elemental distributions during annealing.
Comparable segregation and phase transformation in intact coated and uncoated particles would falsify the proposed protective-shell effect.

contradictions.description: Shell stability and inertness are stated as preconditions for the prediction, yet shell degradation or chemical participation is also classified as falsifying the mechanism. Such degradation would violate the stated boundary conditions rather than directly test whether an intact inert shell suppresses segregation.
